newsitem.title: USA: U.S. calls for speedy Boeing 737 rudder redesign.
newsitem.headline: U.S. calls for speedy Boeing 737 rudder redesign.

text.p: U.S. safety officials on Thursday called for the speedy installation of modified rudders on the popular Boeing Co. 737 and for new training so pilots can try to combat any sudden, unexpected rudder movement.
The recommendations by the National Transportation Safety Board stemmed from investigations of at least two major accidents in which 737s went into uncontrolled rolls and crashed.

One was the USAir flight that went down near Pittsburgh in 1994, killing all 132 people aboard, and the other was the crash of a United Airlines flight near Colorado Springs, Colorado, in 1991, killing all 25 people on board. United is a unit of UAL Corp.
The board has said the 737's rudder system could jam in extreme cold or hot temperatures, but it has not yet determined the causes of the two crashes.

It noted that Boeing and the Federal Aviation Administration said last Jan. 16 that portions of the power control unit of the rudder on 737s would be redesigned and the planes retrofitted within two years.

But the board said it was concerned that the two-year deadline might slip, and it recommended the FAA require the "expeditious" installation of a redesigned main rudder power unit in 737s, about 2,600 of which are now flying worldwide.
Aviation specialists say the 737 has an excellent safety record with only a few accidents in millions of miles flown.

The board also said that an FAA order for new pilot training to cope with sudden rudder movement may not be enough and it should also require that pilots be told that reverse rudder movement can be caused by high-rate pilot rudder imput.
It said reverse rudder movement was seemingly unlikely and pilots would not know how to cope without specific training.

The board recommended that pilots be instructed that high-rate rudder command may result in reverse movement, that continued pressure would only exacerbate it and that aileron/spoiler action could help maintain control of the plane.
FAA officials said they were reviewing the board's recommendations and would act on them as warranted.
